subject: math
title: Greatest Common Factor and Least Common Multiple
seo_title: Grade 6 GCF and LCM Worksheets: Greatest Common Factor, Least Common Multiple, Distributive Property
standard_text: Find the greatest common factor of two whole numbers less than or equal to 100 and the least common multiple of two whole numbers less than or equal to 12. Use the distributive property to express a sum of two whole numbers 1–100 with a common factor as a multiple of a sum of two whole numbers with no common factor. For example, express 36 + 8 as 4 (9 + 2).
meta_desc: Free Grade 6 GCF and LCM worksheets: find the greatest common factor and least common multiple, use prime factorization and factor trees, factor out the GCF with the distributive property, and solve GCF or LCM word problems. 100 practice questions with an answer key.
key_big: The GCF is the biggest number that divides both. The LCM is the first number both divide into.
key_sub: For 6 and 8: the GCF is 2 and the LCM is 24, not 6 × 8 = 48. Use the GCF for equal groups and pieces, the LCM for things that repeat and line up. Factoring out the GCF: 36 + 8 = 4 × (9 + 2).
body_html:
The greatest common factor (GCF)

A common factor divides both numbers. The greatest common factor is the biggest one. List the factors of each number, circle the ones in both lists, and pick the greatest.

Example

Find the GCF of 18 and 45.

Factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. Factors of 45: 1, 3, 5, 9, 15, 45. Common factors: 1, 3, 9.

Answer: 9

The least common multiple (LCM)

A common multiple is in the skip-counting list of both numbers. The least common multiple is the first one. Count by the bigger number and stop at the first multiple of the smaller number.

Example

Find the LCM of 9 and 12.

Count by 12: 12, 24, 36. 12 and 24 are not multiples of 9, but 36 = 9 × 4.

Answer: 36

A shortcut: prime factorization

Split a number into factors until every branch ends in a prime. For the GCF, multiply the primes the two numbers share. For the LCM, use each prime the most times it appears in either number.

Example

24 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 and 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3. Find the GCF.

Shared primes: 2, 2 and 3. Multiply them: 2 × 2 × 3 = 12.

Answer: 12

Factor out the GCF

The distributive property lets you write a sum as a product. Divide both numbers by their GCF and put what is left in parentheses. The two numbers inside should have no common factor except 1.

Example

Rewrite 36 + 8 as a product using the GCF.

The GCF of 36 and 8 is 4. 36 = 4 × 9 and 8 = 4 × 2. 9 and 2 have no common factor.

Answer: 36 + 8 = 4 × (9 + 2)

GCF or LCM?

The problem asks…UseExample
The greatest number of identical groups, kits or teamsGCF24 pencils and 36 erasers make 12 kits
The biggest equal pieces or squares with nothing left overGCF48 cm and 60 cm ribbons: 12 cm pieces
When two repeating events happen together againLCMBuses every 6 and 9 minutes: 18 minutes
The least number to buy so two pack sizes matchLCMPacks of 12 and 8: 24 of each

Check your answer: a GCF is never bigger than the smaller number, and an LCM is never smaller than the bigger number.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Stopping at any common factor: GCF of 30 and 45 is 5Find the greatest one: 15
Multiplying for the LCM: LCM of 6 and 8 is 4848 is a common multiple, but 24 comes first
Mixing up GCF and LCMGroups and pieces: GCF. Repeating and matching: LCM
Thinking the GCF can’t be one of the numbersGCF of 16 and 48 is 16, because 16 × 3 = 48
Factoring out a smaller factor: 36 + 8 = 2 × (18 + 4)18 and 4 still share 2. Use the GCF: 4 × (9 + 2)
Dividing only one number: 36 + 8 = 4 × (9 + 8)Divide both numbers by the GCF

faq.q: How do you find the GCF of two numbers?
faq.a: List the factors of each number and pick the greatest one that is in both lists. For 24 and 36, the common factors are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12, so the GCF is 12.

faq.q: How do you find the LCM of two numbers?
faq.a: Count by the bigger number until you reach a multiple of the smaller number. For 6 and 8, count 8, 16, 24; 24 is a multiple of 6, so the LCM is 24.

faq.q: How do you know whether to use GCF or LCM in a word problem?
faq.a: Use the GCF when you split things into the greatest number of equal groups or the biggest equal pieces. Use the LCM when events repeat and line up again, or when you buy packs so two amounts match.

faq.q: How do you use the distributive property with the GCF?
faq.a: Divide both numbers by their GCF and write the GCF times the sum of what is left. For example, 36 + 8 = 4 × (9 + 2), because the GCF of 36 and 8 is 4.

items.q: Which list shows all the common factors of 12 and 18?
items.e: Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. Factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. Common factors: 1, 2, 3, 6. The greatest is 6. Keep 1 and the GCF in the list, and use only numbers that divide both.

items.q: Which list shows all the common factors of 16 and 40?
items.e: Factors of 16: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Factors of 40: 1, 2, 4, 5, 8, 10, 20, 40. Common factors: 1, 2, 4, 8. The greatest is 8. Keep 1 and the GCF in the list, and use only numbers that divide both.

items.q: Which list shows all the common factors of 30 and 45?
items.e: Factors of 30: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15, 30. Factors of 45: 1, 3, 5, 9, 15, 45. Common factors: 1, 3, 5, 15. The greatest is 15. Keep 1 and the GCF in the list, and use only numbers that divide both.

items.q: Which list shows all the common factors of 24 and 36?
items.e: Factors of 24: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24. Factors of 36: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36. Common factors: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. The greatest is 12. Keep 1 and the GCF in the list, and use only numbers that divide both.

items.q: Which number is a common factor of 36 and 54?
items.e: 9 × 4 = 36 and 9 × 6 = 54, so 9 is a common factor. 4 is a factor of 36 only, 27 is a factor of 54 only, and 108 is a common multiple.

items.q: Which number is a common factor of 42 and 60?
items.e: 6 × 7 = 42 and 6 × 10 = 60, so 6 is a common factor. 7 is a factor of 42 only, 10 is a factor of 60 only, and 420 is a common multiple.

items.q: Which number is not a common factor of 48 and 80?
items.e: 6 is a factor of 48, but 80 ÷ 6 = 13 R 2, so 6 is not a common factor. 2, 8 and 16 divide both numbers.

items.q: Which number is not a common factor of 60 and 90?
items.e: 4 is a factor of 60, but 90 ÷ 4 = 22 R 2, so 4 is not a common factor. 5, 6 and 15 divide both numbers.

items.q: What is the greatest common factor (GCF) of 14 and 21?
items.e: Factors of 14: 1, 2, 7, 14. Factors of 21: 1, 3, 7, 21. Common factors: 1, 7. The greatest is 7. 2 is a factor of 14 only, so it is not a common factor.

items.q: What is the greatest common factor (GCF) of 20 and 30?
items.e: Factors of 20: 1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 20. Factors of 30: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15, 30. Common factors: 1, 2, 5, 10. The greatest is 10. 5 is a common factor too, but not the greatest.

items.q: What is the greatest common factor (GCF) of 18 and 27?
items.e: Factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. Factors of 27: 1, 3, 9, 27. Common factors: 1, 3, 9. The greatest is 9. 3 is a common factor too, but not the greatest.

items.q: What is the greatest common factor (GCF) of 13 and 52?
items.e: Factors of 13: 1, 13. Factors of 52: 1, 2, 4, 13, 26, 52. Common factors: 1, 13. The greatest is 13. 13 divides 52 (13 × 4 = 52), so the smaller number is the GCF.

items.q: What is the greatest common factor (GCF) of 9 and 20?
items.e: Factors of 9: 1, 3, 9. Factors of 20: 1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 20. Common factors: 1. The greatest is 1. 9 and 20 share no factor except 1, so their GCF is 1.

items.q: What is the greatest common factor (GCF) of 28 and 42?
items.e: Factors of 28: 1, 2, 4, 7, 14, 28. Factors of 42: 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 14, 21, 42. Common factors: 1, 2, 7, 14. The greatest is 14. 7 is a common factor too, but not the greatest.

items.q: What is the greatest common factor (GCF) of 48 and 72?
items.e: Factors of 48: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24, 48. Factors of 72: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12, 18, 24, 36, 72. Common factors: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24. The greatest is 24. 12 is a common factor too, but not the greatest.

items.q: What is the greatest common factor (GCF) of 36 and 90?
items.e: Factors of 36: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36. Factors of 90: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 15, 18, 30, 45, 90. Common factors: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. The greatest is 18. 9 is a common factor too, but not the greatest.

items.q: What is the greatest common factor (GCF) of 54 and 81?
items.e: Factors of 54: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18, 27, 54. Factors of 81: 1, 3, 9, 27, 81. Common factors: 1, 3, 9, 27. The greatest is 27. 9 is a common factor too, but not the greatest.

items.q: What is the greatest common factor (GCF) of 64 and 96?
items.e: Factors of 64: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64. Factors of 96: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 96. Common factors: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. The greatest is 32. 16 is a common factor too, but not the greatest.

items.q: Sofia says the GCF of 30 and 45 is 5, because 5 is a factor of both. Is she right?
items.e: 5 is a common factor, but not the greatest. 15 × 2 = 30 and 15 × 3 = 45, so the GCF is 15. 90 is the LCM, and 30 is not a factor of 45.

items.q: Owen says the GCF of 16 and 48 is 16. Is he right?
items.e: 16 × 3 = 48, so 16 is a factor of both numbers, and no factor of 16 is bigger than 16. The GCF can be the smaller number.

items.q: Which list shows the first 3 common multiples of 4 and 6?
items.e: Multiples of 6: 6, 12. Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12. The first number in both lists is 12. The common multiples are the multiples of the LCM: 12, 24, 36. Counting by 4 × 6 = 24 skips 12.

items.q: Which list shows the first 3 common multiples of 6 and 9?
items.e: Multiples of 9: 9, 18. Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18. The first number in both lists is 18. The common multiples are the multiples of the LCM: 18, 36, 54. Counting by 6 × 9 = 54 skips 18.

items.q: Which list shows the first 3 common multiples of 10 and 12?
items.e: Multiples of 12: 12, 24, 36, 48, 60. Multiples of 10: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60. The first number in both lists is 60. The common multiples are the multiples of the LCM: 60, 120, 180. Counting by 10 × 12 = 120 skips 60.

items.q: What is the least common multiple (LCM) of 3 and 4?
items.e: Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12. Multiples of 3: 3, 6, 9, 12. The first number in both lists is 12. 3 and 4 share no factor except 1, so here the LCM is 3 × 4.

items.q: What is the least common multiple (LCM) of 4 and 8?
items.e: Multiples of 8: 8. Multiples of 4: 4, 8. The first number in both lists is 8. 8 is a multiple of 4, so the bigger number is the LCM.

items.q: What is the least common multiple (LCM) of 4 and 10?
items.e: Multiples of 10: 10, 20. Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20. The first number in both lists is 20. 4 × 10 = 40 is a common multiple, but not the least.

items.q: What is the least common multiple (LCM) of 6 and 10?
items.e: Multiples of 10: 10, 20, 30. Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30. The first number in both lists is 30. 6 × 10 = 60 is a common multiple, but not the least.

items.q: What is the least common multiple (LCM) of 5 and 7?
items.e: Multiples of 7: 7, 14, 21, 28, 35. Multiples of 5: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35. The first number in both lists is 35. 5 and 7 share no factor except 1, so here the LCM is 5 × 7.

items.q: What is the least common multiple (LCM) of 8 and 10?
items.e: Multiples of 10: 10, 20, 30, 40. Multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24, 32, 40. The first number in both lists is 40. 8 × 10 = 80 is a common multiple, but not the least.

items.q: What is the least common multiple (LCM) of 9 and 12?
items.e: Multiples of 12: 12, 24, 36. Multiples of 9: 9, 18, 27, 36. The first number in both lists is 36. 9 × 12 = 108 is a common multiple, but not the least.

items.q: What is the least common multiple (LCM) of 4 and 9?
items.e: Multiples of 9: 9, 18, 27, 36. Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32, 36. The first number in both lists is 36. 4 and 9 share no factor except 1, so here the LCM is 4 × 9.

items.q: What is the least common multiple (LCM) of 6 and 12?
items.e: Multiples of 12: 12. Multiples of 6: 6, 12. The first number in both lists is 12. 12 is a multiple of 6, so the bigger number is the LCM.

items.q: What is the least common multiple (LCM) of 3 and 10?
items.e: Multiples of 10: 10, 20, 30. Multiples of 3: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 27, 30. The first number in both lists is 30. 3 and 10 share no factor except 1, so here the LCM is 3 × 10.

items.q: Which number is a common multiple of 3 and 8?
items.e: 48 = 3 × 16 and 48 = 8 × 6, so 48 is a common multiple. 11 is 3 + 8. 32 is a multiple of only one of the numbers, and so is 30.

items.q: Which number is a common multiple of 5 and 6?
items.e: 60 = 5 × 12 and 60 = 6 × 10, so 60 is a common multiple. 11 is 5 + 6. 25 is a multiple of only one of the numbers, and so is 36.

items.q: Which number is not a common multiple of 4 and 10?
items.e: 30 is a multiple of 10, but 30 ÷ 4 = 7 R 2, so 30 is not a multiple of 4. The LCM of 4 and 10 is 20, and 20, 40 and 60 are all multiples of 20.

items.q: Eli says the LCM of 6 and 8 is 48, because 6 × 8 = 48. Is he right?
items.e: Multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24. Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24. The first number in both lists is 24. 48 is a common multiple, but not the least. 2 is the GCF, and 14 is 6 + 8.

items.q: Emma says the LCM of 5 and 10 is 50. Is she right?
items.e: 10 is a multiple of 5 (5 × 2 = 10) and of 10, so the LCM is 10. When one number is a multiple of the other, the bigger number is the LCM.

items.q: For which pair is the LCM equal to the two numbers multiplied together?
items.e: 5 and 8 share no factor except 1, so the LCM is 5 × 8 = 40. The other pairs share a factor: the LCM of 4 and 6 is 12 (not 24), of 6 and 9 is 18 (not 54), and of 8 and 12 is 24 (not 96).

items.q: Which pair of numbers has an LCM of 24?
items.e: Multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24. Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24. So the LCM of 6 and 8 is 24. 4 × 6 = 24 and 2 × 12 = 24, but their LCM is 12. The LCM of 6 and 12 is also 12.

items.q: What is the prime factorization of 36?
items.e: Keep splitting until every branch ends in a prime: 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3. 6 × 6 is not finished, because 6 and 6 are not prime. 1 is not prime, so it is not written.

items.q: What is the prime factorization of 60?
items.e: Keep splitting until every branch ends in a prime: 60 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5. 6 × 10 is not finished, because 6 and 10 are not prime. 1 is not prime, so it is not written.

items.q: What is the prime factorization of 90?
items.e: Keep splitting until every branch ends in a prime: 90 = 2 × 3 × 3 × 5. 9 × 10 is not finished, because 9 and 10 are not prime. 1 is not prime, so it is not written.

items.q: What is the prime factorization of 100?
items.e: Keep splitting until every branch ends in a prime: 100 = 2 × 2 × 5 × 5. 10 × 10 is not finished, because 10 and 10 are not prime. 1 is not prime, so it is not written.

items.q: Which number has the prime factorization 2 × 2 × 3 × 5?
items.e: Multiply all the primes, including the repeated ones: 2 × 2 × 3 × 5 = 60. Adding them gives 12, and using each prime only once gives 30.

items.q: Which number has the prime factorization 2 × 3 × 3 × 5?
items.e: Multiply all the primes, including the repeated ones: 2 × 3 × 3 × 5 = 90. Adding them gives 13, and using each prime only once gives 30.

items.q: Which number has the prime factorization 2 × 2 × 2 × 7?
items.e: Multiply all the primes, including the repeated ones: 2 × 2 × 2 × 7 = 56. Adding them gives 13, and using each prime only once gives 14.

items.q: Which number has the prime factorization 3 × 3 × 7?
items.e: Multiply all the primes, including the repeated ones: 3 × 3 × 7 = 63. Adding them gives 13, and using each prime only once gives 21.

items.q: 24 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 and 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3. What is the GCF of 24 and 36?
items.e: Circle the primes the two lists share: 2 × 2 × 3. Multiply them: 2 × 2 × 3 = 12. Use a shared prime as many times as it appears in both lists. Using each shared prime only once gives 6.

items.q: 45 = 3 × 3 × 5 and 75 = 3 × 5 × 5. What is the GCF of 45 and 75?
items.e: Circle the primes the two lists share: 3 × 5. Multiply them: 3 × 5 = 15. Use a shared prime as many times as it appears in both lists.

items.q: 56 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 7 and 98 = 2 × 7 × 7. What is the GCF of 56 and 98?
items.e: Circle the primes the two lists share: 2 × 7. Multiply them: 2 × 7 = 14. Use a shared prime as many times as it appears in both lists.

items.q: 60 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5 and 84 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 7. What is the GCF of 60 and 84?
items.e: Circle the primes the two lists share: 2 × 2 × 3. Multiply them: 2 × 2 × 3 = 12. Use a shared prime as many times as it appears in both lists. Using each shared prime only once gives 6.

items.q: 8 = 2 × 2 × 2 and 12 = 2 × 2 × 3. What is the LCM of 8 and 12?
items.e: Use each prime the greatest number of times it appears in either list: 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 = 24. 8 × 12 = 96 uses the shared primes twice.

items.q: 9 = 3 × 3 and 12 = 2 × 2 × 3. What is the LCM of 9 and 12?
items.e: Use each prime the greatest number of times it appears in either list: 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 = 36. 9 × 12 = 108 uses the shared primes twice.

items.q: 10 = 2 × 5 and 12 = 2 × 2 × 3. What is the LCM of 10 and 12?
items.e: Use each prime the greatest number of times it appears in either list: 2 × 2 × 3 × 5 = 60. 10 × 12 = 120 uses the shared primes twice.

items.q: Which is true for 4 and 10?
items.e: Factors of 4: 1, 2, 4. Factors of 10: 1, 2, 5, 10. GCF = 2. Multiples of 10: 10, 20. Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20. So LCM = 20. The GCF is never bigger than the numbers, and the LCM is never smaller.

items.q: Which is true for 6 and 9?
items.e: Factors of 6: 1, 2, 3, 6. Factors of 9: 1, 3, 9. GCF = 3. Multiples of 9: 9, 18. Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18. So LCM = 18. The GCF is never bigger than the numbers, and the LCM is never smaller.

items.q: Which is true for 8 and 12?
items.e: Factors of 8: 1, 2, 4, 8. Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. GCF = 4. Multiples of 12: 12, 24. Multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24. So LCM = 24. The GCF is never bigger than the numbers, and the LCM is never smaller.

items.q: Which is true for 6 and 10?
items.e: Factors of 6: 1, 2, 3, 6. Factors of 10: 1, 2, 5, 10. GCF = 2. Multiples of 10: 10, 20, 30. Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30. So LCM = 30. The GCF is never bigger than the numbers, and the LCM is never smaller.

items.q: Which is true for 9 and 12?
items.e: Factors of 9: 1, 3, 9. Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. GCF = 3. Multiples of 12: 12, 24, 36. Multiples of 9: 9, 18, 27, 36. So LCM = 36. The GCF is never bigger than the numbers, and the LCM is never smaller.

sets.title: Factor out the GCF: the distributive property

items.q: The rectangle shows 6 × (5 + 7). Which sum is equal to 6 × (5 + 7)?
items.e: The two parts of the rectangle are 6 × 5 = 30 and 6 × 7 = 42. So 6 × (5 + 7) = 30 + 42. Multiply 6 by both numbers in the parentheses.

items.q: The rectangle shows 3 × (8 + 4). Which sum is equal to 3 × (8 + 4)?
items.e: The two parts of the rectangle are 3 × 8 = 24 and 3 × 4 = 12. So 3 × (8 + 4) = 24 + 12. Multiply 3 by both numbers in the parentheses.

items.q: The rectangle shows 4 × (7 + 5). Which sum is equal to 4 × (7 + 5)?
items.e: The two parts of the rectangle are 4 × 7 = 28 and 4 × 5 = 20. So 4 × (7 + 5) = 28 + 20. Multiply 4 by both numbers in the parentheses.

items.q: The rectangle shows 5 × (6 + 3). Which sum is equal to 5 × (6 + 3)?
items.e: The two parts of the rectangle are 5 × 6 = 30 and 5 × 3 = 15. So 5 × (6 + 3) = 30 + 15. Multiply 5 by both numbers in the parentheses.

items.q: Factor out the GCF to rewrite 24 + 40 as a product.
items.e: The GCF of 24 and 40 is 8. 24 = 8 × 3 and 40 = 8 × 5, so 24 + 40 = 8 × (3 + 5). Check: 3 and 5 have no common factor, and 8 × 8 = 64. 4 × (6 + 10) uses 4, which is not the greatest.

items.q: Factor out the GCF to rewrite 18 + 27 as a product.
items.e: The GCF of 18 and 27 is 9. 18 = 9 × 2 and 27 = 9 × 3, so 18 + 27 = 9 × (2 + 3). Check: 2 and 3 have no common factor, and 9 × 5 = 45. 3 × (6 + 9) uses 3, which is not the greatest.

items.q: Factor out the GCF to rewrite 45 + 60 as a product.
items.e: The GCF of 45 and 60 is 15. 45 = 15 × 3 and 60 = 15 × 4, so 45 + 60 = 15 × (3 + 4). Check: 3 and 4 have no common factor, and 15 × 7 = 105. 5 × (9 + 12) uses 5, which is not the greatest.

items.q: Factor out the GCF to rewrite 56 + 42 as a product.
items.e: The GCF of 56 and 42 is 14. 56 = 14 × 4 and 42 = 14 × 3, so 56 + 42 = 14 × (4 + 3). Check: 4 and 3 have no common factor, and 14 × 7 = 98. 7 × (8 + 6) uses 7, which is not the greatest.

items.q: Factor out the GCF to rewrite 32 + 80 as a product.
items.e: The GCF of 32 and 80 is 16. 32 = 16 × 2 and 80 = 16 × 5, so 32 + 80 = 16 × (2 + 5). Check: 2 and 5 have no common factor, and 16 × 7 = 112. 8 × (4 + 10) uses 8, which is not the greatest.

items.q: Factor out the GCF to rewrite 20 + 50 as a product.
items.e: The GCF of 20 and 50 is 10. 20 = 10 × 2 and 50 = 10 × 5, so 20 + 50 = 10 × (2 + 5). Check: 2 and 5 have no common factor, and 10 × 7 = 70. 5 × (4 + 10) uses 5, which is not the greatest.

items.q: Factor out the GCF to rewrite 63 + 81 as a product.
items.e: The GCF of 63 and 81 is 9. 63 = 9 × 7 and 81 = 9 × 9, so 63 + 81 = 9 × (7 + 9). Check: 7 and 9 have no common factor, and 9 × 16 = 144. 3 × (21 + 27) uses 3, which is not the greatest.

items.q: Factor out the GCF to rewrite 48 + 18 as a product.
items.e: The GCF of 48 and 18 is 6. 48 = 6 × 8 and 18 = 6 × 3, so 48 + 18 = 6 × (8 + 3). Check: 8 and 3 have no common factor, and 6 × 11 = 66. 3 × (16 + 6) uses 3, which is not the greatest.

items.q: 42 + 70 = 14 × (3 + ?). What number is missing?
items.e: 70 ÷ 14 = 5, so the missing number is 5. Check: 14 × (3 + 5) = 14 × 8 = 112 = 42 + 70.

items.q: 36 + 84 = 12 × (3 + ?). What number is missing?
45 + 75 = ? × (3 + 5). What number is missing?
items.e: 45 = 15 × 3 and 75 = 15 × 5, so the missing factor is the GCF, 15. Check: 15 × 8 = 120 = 45 + 75.

items.q: 56 + 98 = ? × (4 + 7). What number is missing?
items.e: 56 = 14 × 4 and 98 = 14 × 7, so the missing factor is the GCF, 14. Check: 14 × 11 = 154 = 56 + 98.

items.q: Zoe factors out the GCF and writes 24 + 36 = 6 × (4 + 6). Is she right?
c: Yes. 6 is a factor of both
items.e: 6 × (4 + 6) is equal to 60, but 4 and 6 still share the factor 2, so 6 is not the GCF. The GCF of 24 and 36 is 12: 24 + 36 = 12 × (2 + 3).

items.q: Grace factors out the GCF and writes 30 + 45 = 15 × (2 + 3). Is she right?
items.e: 15 × 2 = 30 and 15 × 3 = 45, and 2 and 3 have no common factor except 1. So 15 is the GCF and 15 × (2 + 3) is right.

items.q: Nora factors out the GCF and writes 16 + 40 = 8 × (2 + 40). Is she right?
items.e: 8 is the GCF, but both numbers must be divided by 8: 16 ÷ 8 = 2 and 40 ÷ 8 = 5. So 16 + 40 = 8 × (2 + 5). 8 × (2 + 40) = 336, not 56.

items.q: Maya factors out the GCF and writes 27 + 63 = 9 × (3 + 7). Is she right?
items.e: 9 × 3 = 27 and 9 × 7 = 63, and 3 and 7 have no common factor except 1. So 9 is the GCF and 9 × (3 + 7) is right. 3 is a common factor, but not the greatest.

items.q: Omar has 24 pencils and 36 erasers. He wants to make identical kits with nothing left over. What is the greatest number of kits he can make?
items.e: Find the GCF of 24 and 36. Common factors: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. The GCF is 12, so he can make 12 kits, each with 2 pencils and 3 erasers. 6 kits would work too, but 12 is greater.

items.q: Kai has 40 apples and 56 oranges. He wants to make identical baskets with nothing left over. What is the greatest number of baskets he can make?
items.e: Find the GCF of 40 and 56. Common factors: 1, 2, 4, 8. The GCF is 8, so he can make 8 baskets, each with 5 apples and 7 oranges. 280 is the LCM, not the GCF.

items.q: Leo has 16 red roses and 28 white roses. He wants to make identical bouquets with nothing left over. What is the greatest number of bouquets he can make?
items.e: Find the GCF of 16 and 28. Common factors: 1, 2, 4. The GCF is 4, so he can make 4 bouquets, each with 4 red roses and 7 white roses. 7 is the number of white roses in each bouquet.

items.q: A coach has 18 boys and 27 girls. She wants teams that each have the same number of boys and the same number of girls, with no one left out. What is the greatest number of teams?
items.e: Find the GCF of 18 and 27. Common factors: 1, 3, 9. The GCF is 9, so there are 9 teams, each with 2 boys and 3 girls. 45 is 18 + 27, the total number of students.

items.q: Jack has two ribbons, 48 cm and 60 cm long. He cuts both into pieces that are all the same length, with nothing left over. What is the longest each piece can be?
items.e: The length must divide both 48 and 60. Common factors: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. The GCF is 12 cm: 4 pieces from the first ribbon and 5 from the second. 240 is the LCM, longer than both ribbons.

items.q: A garden is 30 ft by 42 ft. Ben wants to split it into equal square plots with no space left over. What is the largest side length the squares can have?
items.e: The side must divide both 30 and 42. Common factors: 1, 2, 3, 6. The GCF is 6 ft, which gives 5 rows of 7 squares. 210 is the LCM, and it is bigger than the garden.

items.q: Paper plates come in packs of 12 and cups come in packs of 8. Ruby wants the same number of plates and cups. What is the least number of each she can buy?
items.e: Multiples of 12: 12, 24. Multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24. The first number in both lists is 24. So she buys 24 of each: 2 packs of plates and 3 packs of cups. 12 × 8 = 96 also works, but it is not the least.

items.q: A red light flashes every 4 seconds and a blue light flashes every 10 seconds. They flash together now. In how many seconds will they next flash together?
items.e: Multiples of 10: 10, 20. Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20. The first number in both lists is 20. 4 × 10 = 40 is a later time they flash together, and 2 is the GCF.

items.q: Lily waters her plants every 4 days. Luis waters his plants every 6 days. They both water today. In how many days will they both water on the same day again?
items.e: Multiples of 6: 6, 12. Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12. The first number in both lists is 12. 4 × 6 = 24 days is not the first time, and 10 is 4 + 6.

items.q: Sam runs one lap of a track in 3 minutes. Noah runs one lap in 5 minutes. They start together at the starting line. After how many minutes will they both be at the starting line again?
items.e: Multiples of 5: 5, 10, 15. Multiples of 3: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15. The first number in both lists is 15. 3 and 5 share no factor except 1, so the LCM is 3 × 5. 8 is 3 + 5.

items.q: Juice boxes come in packs of 6 and granola bars come in packs of 10. Ava wants the same number of juice boxes and granola bars. What is the least number of each she can buy?
items.e: Multiples of 10: 10, 20, 30. Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30. The first number in both lists is 30. That is 5 packs of juice and 3 packs of granola bars. 6 × 10 = 60 works, but it is not the least.

items.q: Bus A leaves the station every 6 minutes. Bus B leaves every 9 minutes. Both buses leave at 8:00 a.m. When will they next leave at the same time?
items.e: Multiples of 9: 9, 18. Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18. The first number in both lists is 18. So they leave together again 18 minutes later, at 8:18 a.m. 6 × 9 = 54 minutes is not the first time, and 6 + 9 = 15 is not a multiple of 6.

items.q: Sofia has 36 pens and 48 stickers. She wants to make the greatest number of identical gift bags with nothing left over. What should she find?
items.e: She is splitting things into equal groups, and the number of bags must divide both 36 and 48. That is the GCF (12 bags).

items.q: A green light blinks every 8 seconds and a yellow light blinks every 12 seconds. They blink together now. To find when they next blink together, what should you find?
items.e: The times repeat and must line up again, so you need a common multiple: the LCM (24 seconds). 8 × 12 = 96 is a common multiple, but not the first.

items.q: Owen cuts an 18 in by 24 in sheet of paper into equal squares that are as big as possible, with none left over. What should he find?
items.e: The side of each square must divide both 18 and 24, and it must be as big as possible. That is the GCF (6 in).

items.q: Hot dogs come in packs of 10 and buns come in packs of 8. Eli wants the same number of hot dogs and buns. To find the least number of each, what should he find?
items.e: The totals are multiples of 10 and of 8, and they must match. That is the LCM (40).

items.q: Emma has 30 markers and 45 crayons. She makes the greatest number of identical art kits with nothing left over. How many crayons are in each kit?
items.e: The GCF of 30 and 45 is 15, so there are 15 kits. 45 ÷ 15 = 3 crayons in each kit (and 30 ÷ 15 = 2 markers). 15 is the number of kits, not crayons.

items.q: Star stickers come in sheets of 9 and heart stickers come in sheets of 12. Zoe wants the same number of star and heart stickers, as few as possible. How many sheets of star stickers should she buy?
items.e: Multiples of 12: 12, 24, 36. Multiples of 9: 9, 18, 27, 36. The first number in both lists is 36. She needs 36 star stickers: 36 ÷ 9 = 4 sheets. 3 sheets is the number of heart sticker sheets (36 ÷ 12).

items.q: A class has 24 boys and 40 girls. They form 8 teams, and each team has the same number of boys and the same number of girls. Which expression shows all the students?
items.e: Each team has 24 ÷ 8 = 3 boys and 40 ÷ 8 = 5 girls, so 24 + 40 = 8 × (3 + 5) = 64. 4 × (6 + 10) is also 64, but it shows 4 teams, not 8.

items.q: A florist has 45 roses and 60 tulips. She makes the greatest number of identical bouquets with nothing left over. How many flowers are in each bouquet?
items.e: The GCF of 45 and 60 is 15, so there are 15 bouquets. Each has 45 ÷ 15 = 3 roses and 60 ÷ 15 = 4 tulips: 3 + 4 = 7 flowers. 21 comes from using 5 bouquets, which is not the greatest.
